s.en: run a command with substitute user and group ID
s.es: cambia de usuario (por defecto a root) abriendo una shell

tip.es: «su -» pide la contraseña del usuario destino (root); «sudo -i» pide la tuya.
tip.en: "su -" asks for the target user's password (root); "sudo -i" asks for yours.

o.es: Shell de login: entorno limpio y directorio personal del usuario destino (igual que escribir «su -»).
o.en: Login shell: clean environment and the target user's home (same as typing "su -").

o.es: Ejecuta ese comando y vuelve, en lugar de abrir una shell interactiva.
o.en: Run that command and return, instead of an interactive shell.

o.es: Usa esa shell en vez de la del usuario.
o.en: Run the specified shell instead of the user's default.

o.es: Conserva las variables de entorno actuales.

o.en: Pass -f to the shell, which may or may not be useful, depending on the shell.
Specify a supplementary group. This option is available to the root user only. The first specified supplementary group is also used as a primary group if the option --group is not specified.

Create a pseudo-terminal for the session. The independent terminal provides better security as the user does not share a terminal with the original session. Please note security advice about TIOCSTI vulnerability below. The entire session can also be moved to the background (e.g., su --pty - user -c application &).
Same as -c, but do not create a new session. (Discouraged.) Please note security advice about TIOCSTI vulnerability below.
Do not create a pseudo-terminal, opposite of --pty and -P. Please note security advice about TIOCSTI vulnerability below.

Don’t reset the environment variables specified in the comma-separated list when clearing the environment for --login. The whitelist is ignored for the environment variables HOME, SHELL, USER, LOGNAME, and PATH.
